newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: UN body looks at fast-growing space debris risk.
newsitem.headline: UN body looks at fast-growing space debris risk.

text.p: The number of defunct satellites and other clutter in space will multiply dramatically in the next 100 years, aggravating the risk of space collision unless action is taken soon, a U.N. space forum heard this week.

"If we continue to send up the same number of spacecraft in the next 100 years we can expect the number of debris to increase fourfold," said Joerg Bendisch at the Institute for Flight Mechanics and Spaceflight Technology, Germany.

The two-day forum in Vienna is part of a five-year work plan begun in 1996 aimed at setting up internationally binding regulations to reduce space debris which poses a growing threat to astronauts and expensive equipment.
Some 8,000 objects bigger than 10 cm currently orbit the earth, from large spacecraft down to nuts and bolts which have fallen off satellites and fragments from explosions.

"If you have a 10 cm particle impacting a spacecraft at 45,000 km per hour you have no spacecraft anymore," Bendisch told Reuters. "If you have a 1.0 cm aluminium particle impacting a spacecraft it's like a hand grenade."
"We need to find regulations to bring rocket stages and satellites down from the low earth orbit (200 km from the earth), but at this time there is no requirement to do that."

The U.N. body hopes to ensure that anyone launching a space craft must remove it after its mission, where possible, and reroute defunct machines from "prime parking slots" to higher, less desirable orbits.

A number of countries have recently expressed concern that the geostationary orbit -- a band 36,000 km from the earth where most broadcasting and commercial satellites revolve -- is becoming jammed with debris.
Bendisch said the only feasible solution at present for spent satellites that could not be brought back to earth was to send them to a "graveyard orbit" some 300 km beyond the key geostationary band.
The forum will also look at preventing explosions, which disperse thousands of fragments into space, by making spacecraft vent their fuel after use.
Bendisch said there had been over 100 explosions in the past 30 years from machines carrying fuel that were unable to withstand the extreme temperatures of space.
"Each mass you send up there is like orbital dynamite because it is waiting to collide or explode," he noted.
By Bendisch's calculations satellites will risk being bombarded by any one of around 35,000 objects speeding through space in 100 years unless international rules are laid down.

Space debris detectors will be placed on the Russian Mir space station in 1999, the U.N. said. But Bendisch said radar cannot always detect minute particles, and the best solution was to minimise the occurrence of space debris.
"It is important not to spoil outer space which is a resource for mankind for future generations," he said.
